correctness.rationale: The forest obstruction is derived directly: a hypothetical periodic orbit yields a voluntary breakup x leaving y; restoring the worse partner y forces an earlier involuntary loss of a partner z ranked above y, so z must voluntarily leave x. Iterating yields an infinite nonbacktracking walk in a finite forest, contradiction. A mutual-first-choice pair cannot be dissolved; a feedback set of such pairs allows at most f new-edge events interspersed with forest-only stages. Each stage obeys the verified Fanelli–Moscardelli Theorem 4 bound floor(n^3/8). For a simple cycle, a nonuniform binary local preference orientation contains a +-to-- edge, which is mutual first-choice, while each of the two uniform orientations admits a concrete n-step rotating single-edge improvement cycle. This proves exact counting and the stated odd/even stable-existence corollary. Full finite transition enumerator tested all 2040 strict profiles on C3..C10 and 824616 directed moves; this is corroboration, not infinite proof.

originality.rationale: Claim-level search found no equivalently broad dynamics criterion: the motivating ECAI article proves forest convergence, and gives a single 4-cycle failing trajectory, not an exact all-cycle all-preference classification. The local mutual-top feedback sufficient condition and quantified cycle dichotomy are not logical consequences of the reported forest-only theorem without the new freezing and orientation arguments. Database closest results concern complete-preference small markets or static matchings, not global improvement dynamics on arbitrary simple cycles. value.rationale: Graph topology between forests and complete acceptability graphs is an explicit open direction in the motivating paper. The first fundamental cyclic topology receives a natural complete classification over every vertex count and every strict local preference profile, with exactly two failure profiles and exponentially small failure probability under an explicit uniform model. The feedback-set mechanism extends insight to multiple-cycle graphs when preferences freeze a cycle-hitting set. The result distinguishes static stable existence from universal adversarial-order convergence and is structurally motivated rather than a small finite re-enumeration.
